title: Review of Related Anatomy and Physiology of the Nervous System
path: Management of Clients with Neurologic Disorders
Review of Related Anatomy and Physiology

headings.title: Introduction to the Nervous System and Its General Functions
headings.content: The nervous system is the body's primary control and communication network, working rapidly to maintain homeostasis and coordinate all physiological activities. Structurally and functionally, it is divided into the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The general functions of the nervous system are traditionally categorized into three overlapping phases: sensory input, integration, and motor output. Sensory receptors located both internally and externally monitor changes, known as stimuli, and relay this environmental information as electrical signals toward the CNS. Once these signals arrive at the CNS, integration occurs. Integration involves the processing, analysis, and interpretation of the sensory data, determining an appropriate response based on past experiences and current states. Finally, the CNS initiates motor output by activating effector organs, which include muscles and glands, to elicit a specific reaction. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these foundational physiological pathways is critical when assessing patients presenting with neurological deficits, neuropathies, or altered levels of consciousness. By grasping how stimuli translate into coordinated body responses, nurses can better anticipate clinical symptoms, localize potential lesions or dysfunctions, and provide targeted care that supports patient recovery and optimal physiological functioning across various healthcare settings.

headings.title: Central Nervous System: Structure and Function of the Brain
headings.content: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises the brain and the spinal cord, serving as the command center for the entire human body. The brain itself is anatomically and functionally subdivided into several key regions: the cerebrum, the cerebellum, and the brainstem. The cerebrum, the largest part of the brain, is divided into two hemispheres and further separated into four major lobes—frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. Each lobe handles distinct higher-level cognitive functions, such as voluntary motor control, sensory perception, language comprehension, and visual processing. Beneath the cerebrum lies the cerebellum, which is crucially responsible for coordinating voluntary movements, maintaining posture, and ensuring balance and smooth motor execution. The brainstem, consisting of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata, regulates vital, non-conscious autonomic functions such as respiration, heart rate, blood pressure, and basic reflex centers like swallowing and vomiting. For nursing students, mastering the structural geography of the brain is essential. When conducting a neurological assessment, recognizing which specific brain region is affected allows nurses to accurately correlate clinical manifestations—such as aphasia, ataxia, or respiratory depression—with underlying pathology, thereby aiding the multidisciplinary healthcare team in formulating effective patient care plans.

headings.title: Central Nervous System: Structure and Function of the Spinal Cord
headings.content: The spinal cord is a vital, cylindrical bundle of nervous tissue extending from the brainstem down through the vertebral canal, serving as the major communication highway between the brain and the rest of the body. Structurally, it is organized into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal segments, giving rise to paired spinal nerves. Cross-sectional anatomy of the spinal cord reveals an inner core of grey matter, shaped roughly like a butterfly or the letter 'H', surrounded by outer white matter. The grey matter contains neuronal cell bodies, unmyelinated axons, and neuroglia, functioning as a processing center for local reflexes and the integration of incoming and outgoing signals. Conversely, the white matter consists of myelinated nerve fibers organized into ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) tracts that transmit nerve impulses to and from the brain. The spinal cord also manages critical reflex arcs, which allow rapid, involuntary responses to harmful stimuli without waiting for conscious brain processing. For Nigerian nursing professionals, understanding spinal cord anatomy is paramount when caring for patients with traumatic spinal injuries, herniated discs, or degenerative spinal disorders. Identifying the specific level of a spinal lesion helps predict patterns of paralysis, sensory loss, and autonomic dysfunction, guiding prompt nursing interventions and preventative care for complications like pressure ulcers.

headings.title: Peripheral Nervous System: Somatic and Autonomic Divisions
headings.content: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects the central nervous system to the rest of the body, encompassing all neural structures outside the brain and spinal cord. Functionally, the PNS is divided into two primary divisions: the somatic nervous system and the autonomic nervous system. The somatic nervous system consists of sensory neurons that convey information from special sense receptors and skin to the CNS, and motor neurons that conduct impulses from the CNS exclusively to skeletal muscles. This pathway operates under conscious, voluntary control, allowing precise movements of the musculoskeletal system. In contrast, the autonomic nervous system (ANS) regulates involuntary physiological processes, including visceral functions of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and various glands. The ANS is further subdivided into the sympathetic nervous system, which mobilizes the body during stress or physical exertion ('fight or flight'), and the parasympathetic nervous system, which promotes maintenance activities and energy conservation ('rest and digest'). For nursing students, distinguishing between somatic and autonomic functions is indispensable when performing comprehensive patient assessments. Nurses must recognize signs of somatic weakness, such as motor drop or loss of deep tendon reflexes, alongside autonomic alterations like abnormal heart rate, blood pressure fluctuations, or altered gastrointestinal motility, facilitating early detection of neuropathies or systemic shock.

headings.title: Cellular Organization: Neurons and Neuroglial Cells
headings.content: The nervous system is cellularly organized into two primary types of cells: neurons and neuroglial cells. Neurons are the structural and functional units of the nervous system, specialized for the generation and transmission of electrical signals across long distances. A typical mature neuron features a cell body (soma) containing the nucleus, branching dendrites that receive incoming signals from other neurons, and a single axon that transmits electrical impulses away from the cell body toward target cells. Surrounding and supporting the neurons are neuroglial cells, or glia, which greatly outnumber neurons and provide metabolic support, insulation, protection, and physical structure. In the central nervous system, neuroglia include astrocytes (which form the blood-brain barrier and regulate the extracellular environment), oligodendrocytes (which myelinate CNS axons), microglia (which act as phagocytic immune cells), and ependymal cells (which line fluid-filled ventricles). In the peripheral nervous system, supporting cells include Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral axons, and satellite cells, which surround and support neuron cell bodies in ganglia. For nursing students, understanding this cellular organization is vital when studying neuropathology, demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis, or central nervous system infections. Recognizing how damage to oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells disrupts neural transmission equips nurses to better understand clinical symptoms and targeted pharmacological interventions.

headings.title: Neurotransmission and Action Potential Generation
headings.content: Neurotransmission and action potential generation form the electrochemical basis of communication within the nervous system. At rest, a neuron maintains a resting membrane potential, typically around -70 mV, where the inside of the cell is negatively charged relative to the outside, largely maintained by sodium-potassium pumps. When a stimulus reaches a neuron and depolarizes the membrane to a critical threshold level, voltage-gated sodium channels open rapidly, allowing sodium ions to rush into the cell. This influx causes a sudden, dramatic reversal of the membrane potential known as an action potential, or nerve impulse, which propagates down the axon. Following depolarization, voltage-gated potassium channels open, allowing potassium ions to exit the cell, repolarizing the membrane back toward its resting state. Once the action potential reaches the axon terminal of the presynaptic neuron, it triggers the influx of calcium ions, causing vesicles containing neurotransmitters to fuse with the membrane and release their chemical messengers across the synaptic cleft. These neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the postsynaptic cell membrane, exciting or inhibiting it. For nursing students, understanding this electrochemical process is essential for comprehending how various drugs—such as anesthetics, anticonvulsants, and neurotransmitter reuptake inhibitors—exert their therapeutic effects by altering ion channels or synaptic transmission.

headings.title: Protective Structures: Meninges, Ventricles, and Cerebrospinal Fluid
headings.content: The delicate tissues of the central nervous system require extensive protection against physical trauma, mechanical shock, and biochemical imbalances. This protection is provided by three main structures: the protective cranial bones and vertebral column, the meninges, and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained within a system of ventricles. The meninges consist of three continuous connective tissue membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord: the tough, outermost dura mater; the middle, web-like arachnoid mater; and the delicate, vascular innermost pia mater that clings tightly to the CNS surface. Between the arachnoid mater and pia mater lies the subarachnoid space, which is filled with CSF. Cerebrospinal fluid is a clear, colorless liquid produced primarily by the choroid plexuses within the brain's ventricles. It circulates through the ventricles, flows into the subarachnoid space, and cushions the brain, provides buoyancy, and supplies essential nutrients while removing metabolic waste products. For nursing students, clinical knowledge of these structures is vital when evaluating conditions such as meningitis (inflammation of the meninges), hydrocephalus (abnormal accumulation of CSF in the ventricles), or performing diagnostic procedures such as a lumbar puncture. Recognizing symptoms like nuchal rigidity, severe headache, or altered intracranial pressure enables nurses to intervene safely and effectively.

headings.title: Clinical Implications for Nursing Assessment of Neurological Function
headings.content: A thorough neurological assessment is a cornerstone of comprehensive nursing practice, enabling nurses to detect acute changes in neurological status, localize central and peripheral deficits, and evaluate treatment efficacy. Clinical assessment of the nervous system systematically evaluates mental status, cranial nerve function, motor function, sensory function, and reflexes. Evaluating mental status involves assessing level of consciousness, orientation, memory, and cognitive performance, frequently utilizing validated tools such as the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) to monitor patients with traumatic brain injury or stroke. Assessment of the twelve cranial nerves provides direct insight into brainstem integrity and local cerebral function through simple bedside tests of vision, pupillary light reflex, facial movement, and swallowing. Motor and sensory assessments evaluate muscle strength, tone, symmetry, coordination, and tactile or pain sensitivity across all extremities, helping differentiate upper motor neuron lesions from lower motor neuron disorders. Additionally, testing deep tendon reflexes provides crucial data regarding spinal cord and peripheral nerve pathway health. For nursing students in Nigeria, mastering these assessment techniques ensures early identification of critical complications like increased intracranial pressure (ICP), cerebral ischemia, or spinal shock, ultimately empowering nurses to advocate for prompt medical intervention and improved patient outcomes.
